entries.title: Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war
entries.summary: For years, Pakistan supported the Taliban in Afghanistan. But now Pakistan is bombing its neighbor. How the former allies became adversaries and why negotiations keep failing.
entries.content:
Middle East

Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war

October 3, 2026

For years, Pakistan supported the Taliban in Afghanistan. But now Pakistan is bombing its neighbor. How the former allies became adversaries and why negotiations keep failing.

On Thursday night, Pakistan attacked targets in Afghanistan. The results of that attack are disputed. The Taliban, the Islamic fundamentalist nationalist movement that controls Afghanistan, says that between nine and 10 civilians were killed, including women and children. But Pakistan claims the strike killed 22 militants and destroyed weapons and ammunition depots.

These early October attacks are just the latest escalation in a conflict between the two countries that reignited mid-September, after months of comparative calm.

The conflict was sparked again after a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces. On September 18, an attack on a police compound in the northwestern city of Kohat resulted in the deaths of 31 people and more than 100 injured. A splinter group belonging to the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, claimed responsibility for the attack in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bordering Afghanistan.

Pakistan accused Afghanistan of providing the TTP with a safe haven. Afghanistan denies this but clashes at the border and then airstrikes by Pakistan followed.

TTP and Taliban: A complex relationship

The TTP in Pakistan is not the same as Afghanistan's Taliban. Although it does have close ideological and personnel ties to the Afghan Taliban, it is an independent organization that fights the Pakistani state.

Many of its fighters sided with the Taliban during that country's long-running insurgency against international and US troops. This is why, after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the TTP gained more room and more leverage. This has meant that Afghanistan — a former ally of Pakistan — has increasingly become a threat to its neighbor.

Pakistan has asked the Taliban to take action against the TTP, but the close connection between the two make this difficult.

"Because of these personal connections and networks, it is extremely difficult for the Afghan Taliban to break away," says Conrad Schetter, director of the Bonn International Center for Conflict Studies, or BICC.

The connections don't mean that the Taliban has any control over the TTP. There are certainly historical connections between the two, but Schetter doesn't believe that equals any sort of strong, direct influence.

"The Taliban are simply not prepared to take orders from Islamabad," adds Thomas Ruttig, co-director of the Afghanistan Analysts Network, a think tank working between Kabul and Berlin. "They won't let anyone outside interfere."

This means the Pakistani policy of supporting the Taliban in order to gain influence in Afghanistan hasn't worked.

Difficult borders

There's also another older conflict that has an impact on the current situation. This involves what is known as the Durand Line, drawn in 1893 by a British diplomat and an Afghan emir to mark spheres of influence between British India and Afghanistan.

The current border between Afghanistan and Pakistan follows the Durand Line and also divides an area on both sides, homeland to Pashtuns, who make up the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan and second largest in Pakistan.

So the border dispute here isn't just about territory, it's also about identity.

"Ethnic and nationalist elements play a significant role in the conflict," Schetter tells DW. Many Pashtuns still refuse to accept the border that the Durand Line created.

In Pakistan, the country's long-running rivalry with India also plays a part. A friendly Afghanistan would have been advantageous for Pakistan. But India has also strengthened its ties to the Taliban.

"While Islamabad once viewed Afghanistan as a source of 'strategic depth' in its rivalry with India, it now increasingly views its north-western neighbor as a liability," an analysis by British think tank Chatham House notes.

Pakistan exerts pressure

Pakistan still has power over Afghanistan, though. As a landlocked country, Afghanistan relies on trade routes through neighboring countries, and Pakistan in particular. Pakistan can use border closures and trade restrictions to exert pressure even as the Taliban regime is trying to reduce dependence on Pakistan and find new economic and political partners.

Trade and security considerations are now becoming tangled. Pakistan has held talks with the TTP that were mediated by the Taliban and ceasefires were agreed upon. Talks between Pakistan and Afghanistan also took place. But none of the temporary agreements resolved the crucial question of how to prevent attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory.

So in parallel with diplomacy, Pakistan has also been relying on economic and political pressure, for example, by closing borders and restricting trade and by sending Afghan refugees back into Afghanistan.

An analysis by the US-based Council on Foreign Relations notes that the Taliban are worried that if they crack down on the TTP too hard, they will drive the group towards another extremist militant group, the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or IS-K. This group opposes the Taliban.

The conflict recently escalated to another level. At the end of September, Kabul reported 28 killed and 32 captured fighters who had infiltrated Afghanistan from Nuristan province, Pakistan. The Taliban accused Pakistan of supporting its armed opponents, something Pakistan has denied.

"It is known from past decades that Pakistan has regularly supported armed groups on the Afghan side — for example, the Mujahideen during the Soviet occupation and later the Taliban," Ruttig points out. "What's new though is that Pakistan apparently also supports parts of today's armed anti-Taliban opposition."

Significant escalation

This is turning the dispute over the TTP into a larger conflict in which both sides accuse each other of supporting armed groups from the other's territory.

British think tank Chatham House speaks of a significant escalation compared to previous border skirmishes. Worryingly, a conflict over armed groups and border incidents is turning into a direct confrontation between the two nation states.

Ruttig believes that it would be possible to contain the spiraling violence if both sides return to negotiations.

"If both sides were willing to return to the negotiating table — perhaps with international mediation —there would be ways to contain the conflict and, above all, to protect the civilian population on both sides," he argues.

In a late September commentary in Pakistani weekly magazine The Friday Times, Pakistani analyst Saqib Ali Khan advocates for several things that could ease the tensions. That includes a reliable channel between Islamabad and Kabul, a separate approach for armed groups and greater involvement of the population along the border.

The conflict, he argues, is not merely a dispute between two governments but also a security, border, economic and regional conflict.

"Along those lines, there would have to be a shift in perspective on both sides," Schetter concludes.

In the long term, greater economic integration is also needed, he adds, so that Pakistan and Afghanistan do not define their relationship solely through security and power issues.

This story was originally published in German.

entries.title: Tennessee's prison chief resigns after botched execution of murderer Christa Pike
entries.summary: Prison commissioner Frank Strada insisted his team followed protocol, even after two doses of anesthetic failed to kill convicted murderer Christa Pike. He is set to leave his post this month.
entries.content:
October 3, 2026

Prison commissioner Frank Strada insisted his team followed protocol, even after two doses of anesthetic failed to kill convicted murderer Christa Pike. He is set to leave his post this month.

The head of the prison system in the US state of Tennessee is resigning after the execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike went wrong, the state governor said Saturday.

Witnesses said Pike was still breathing and moaning after two doses of the anesthetic pentobarbital failed to kill her during Wednesday's procedure.

The attempt was halted and she was transferred to hospital in critical condition.

It was the second time this year that an execution in the southern state had to be halted.

What do we know about the resignation?

Governor Bill Lee said in a statement that prison commissioner Frank Strada would leave his post sometime this month.

Lee said he thanked Strada for "his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment."

In the same statement, Strada acknowledged that: "Stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward."

He said the department had carried out its responsibilities in accordance with established protocol, but called the review "entirely appropriate and necessary."

The state has halted further executions until the review has been completed.

Strada took on the role in January 2023. Nearly two years later, he announced that Tennessee would, from then on, only use pentobarbital for lethal injections of death-row inmates.

What went wrong?

Tennessee authorities have yet to explain why Pike survived.

Her attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.

Pike's lawyers said Friday that she is unconsciousand on a ventilator in hospital.

While they welcomed Strada's departure, her legal team said, “It does nothing to help Christa now.”

"What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," the four-lawyer team said.

"We hope the governor's call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system," it added.

Had the drugs killed Pike, she would have been the first woman executed by the state since 1820.

Pike was sentenced to death in 1996, aged 20, for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, whom Pike was convinced was trying to steal her boyfriend.

Slemmer, who was 19, was tortured and killed in a remote area near the University of Tennessee in Knoxville.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Latvia: Ruling party leads in exit polls amid populist gains
entries.summary: According to an exit poll by public broadcaster LSM, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centerist party, United List, was projected to win 35.6% of the vote.
entries.content:
Latvia

Latvia: Ruling party leads in exit polls amid populist gains

Published October 3, 2026last updated October 3, 2026

According to an exit poll by public broadcaster LSM, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centerist party, United List, was projected to win 35.6% of the vote.

The party of Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs took a comfortable lead in parliamentary elections on Saturday, exit polls showed.

Kulbergs' centerist, pro-Ukraine party, United List, was projected to win 35.6% of the vote, according to an exit poll by public proadcaster LSM.

"It's remarkably ‌good. ​I was not expecting such result," Kulbergs said at his party's headquarters in Riga.

The exit poll put the the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3% — nearly double its share at the last election in 2022. It had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority.

Kulbergs said on Saturday night that he would not cooperate with any pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out forming a coaltition with Latvia First.

Some 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

The election, which saw 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, has been dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus.

Kulbergs, has only been in office since May after the previous government collapsed over a dispute about Ukrainian drones. Despite his party leading opinion polls, his coalition is expected to emerge weakened as populist parties gain.

Latvia vote shaped by Russia concerns

Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority.

Unlike Ukraine, however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO.

Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere.

Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges.

Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging.

German Eurofighter jets in Latvian airspace

Nevertheless, no parties are proposing any major deviation from Latvia's clear foreign policy alignment with the EU and NATO.

Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets have been deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga.

Once ballots are counted, attention is likely to shift quickly to coalition negotiations, which could prove lengthy and complex.

Partial results are expected on Saturday evening, with preliminary official results due on Sunday.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Ukraine to step up oil attacks as Russia hits Kyiv bridges
entries.summary: As Moscow intensifies attacks on Kyiv and other cities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to hit Russian energy infrastructure.
entries.content:
Published October 3, 2026last updated October 3, 2026

As Moscow intensifies attacks on Kyiv and other cities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to hit Russian energy infrastructure.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday vowed to continue hitting Russia's oil refineries in retaliation for what he called Moscow's new strategy of targeting major Ukrainian cities for intensive air strikes.

Ukraine has accused the Kremlin of stepping up attacks on civilian targets in recent days, to force residents to leave urban areas of the country before winter.

In strikes over the past two days, Russian forces have also hit two major bridges crossing the Dnipro River in the capital, Kyiv.

What did Zelenskyy say?

In an interview with Reuters news agency, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence agencies had uncovered details of a "new doctrine" from Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelenskyy warned.

The Ukrainian leader said that Kyiv would "respond in any way (we can) ... First of all, oil refiners: who give money to them [Russia] for this war. But we will not respond, of course, like them, on any ‌civilian objects."

Second Kyiv bridge struck

This week marks the first time Moscow has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Saturday that the Northern Bridge over the river was struck by Russian forces from the air.

In a statement posted on Telegram, Klitschko said two people were injured and the road surface and trolleybus wires on the bridge were damaged.

"Traffic across the bridge from the left bank to the right bank is currently blocked," he said.

Over the past two days, Kyiv's Southern Bridge has been hit several times by a volley of strikes by Russian drones.

The attacks caused traffic chaos, with long lines of stationary cars and buses clogging major roads.

A total of eight bridges connect Kyiv's western and eastern banks along the Dnipro River.

Russia urges foreign diplomats, nationals to leave Kyiv

Russia's Foreign Ministry on Saturday, meanwhile, warned foreign diplomats and nationals in Kyiv to leave the city, adding that "individuals are knowingly exposing themselves to mortal danger."

"The Armed Forces of the Russian Federation will continue to deliver massive retaliatory strikes," it said, while adding that "responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning."

In the years following its February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has frequently targeted Kyiv with overnight drone attacks.

Moscow has previously denied a systematic targeting of civilians during its bombings.

Moldova denounces latest Russian strike on Ukraine

Moldovan President Maia Sandu condemned the latest Russian attack on Kyiv and complained about a violation of her country's airspace.

"Its war is dangerously reaching Moldova," Sandu said in a post on X. "5 Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated our airspace and exploded on our soil."

"Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped," Sandu said.

The Moldovan Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador and urged Moscow to prevent such incidents.

Moldova is a strong supporter of Ukraine, and its airspace is frequently violated due to Russian attacks on its neighbor.

Russian forces are stationed in the Moldovan breakaway province of Transnistria, raising fears that Moldova could be the next target of invasion after Ukraine.    

Edited by: Natalie Muller, Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot
entries.summary: The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester.
entries.content:
October 3, 2026

The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester.

Two Iranian nationals charged with plotting acts of terrorism  against the United Kingdom's Jewish community were remanded in custody by a court in London on Saturday.

The pair were detained on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

The case only came to light on Friday when the two men were charged, just days after another terror plot, which the UK has linked to Iran, was foiled.

What do we know about the case?

Prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court that Rahman S., 34, and Salam ‌A., 36, are accused of carrying out "hostile reconnaissance" on Jewish targets in Manchester, northern England.

He said the two men planned to use a "homemade explosive device" and had allegedly been in contact with a third party, an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran.

The contact is alleged to have given the pair instructions on how ‌to put together a homemade device from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard.

Luckett said the two suspects had used online resources, including images, plans and maps, to identify and research potential attack sites.

He told the court that the targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue, where two Jewish worshippers were killed in a knife attack a year ago on Friday.

The two Iranian suspects had arrived in Britain in small boats that crossed the English Channel from mainland Europe, Luckett added.

One had been granted asylum, while the other's application is still pending, the court heard.

The pair did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey on October 23.

Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat.

Police find no link to RAF Fairford plot

Evans also said the Manchester plot was "not connected in any way" to the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford last weekend, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said showed "strong indications" of Iranian involvement.

Also on Saturday, police said a dual British-Iranian national, arrested on Thursday in connection with the RAF Fairford plot, was released on police bail.

The 25-year-old was the sixth person arrested and then bailed as the investigation continues.

Police said the five other men held are all British nationals in their 20s and from London.

Police uncovered the RAF Fairford plot when a farmer spotted suspicious white vans near the base early on Sunday morning and called the authorities. Officers found petrol inside the vans, but no explosives.

UK media reported this week that one of the suspects dialled the police about an hour earlier, though that has not been confirmed.

Tehran has rejected as baseless accusations of targeting RAF Fairford, which lies 90 miles (145 kilometers) west of London and has been used by US bombers to strike Iran.

The UK remains on high alert for potential threats from Russia and Iran.

Iran has previously used proxies to commit crimes on British soil, including repeated attacks and plots against Jewish targets, as well as against dissidents.

Antisemitic attacks more broadly have risen sharply since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Spain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down
entries.summary: Organizers estimated that 500,000 people turned out in the streets of Madrid to demand affordable housing. Similar protests were held in around 50 other Spanish cities.
entries.content:
Spain

Spain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down

October 3, 2026

Organizers estimated that 500,000 people turned out in the streets of Madrid to demand affordable housing. Similar protests were held in around 50 other Spanish cities.

Tens of thousands of people protested across Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing.

The protests come a day after the Spanish parliament narrowly voted down two emergency bills designed to support renters and prevent evictions.

"It only proves that it is us the people who have to adapt ‌to the political parties, and not the politicians to ‌what ​the people want, and this can't go on like that," one 26-year-old protester in Madrid told the Reuters news agency.

They are the latest demonstrations in a week-long wave of actions that began in response to the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascalin, in Madrid.

"What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven't seen in a long time, and energy that is showing that eight days of people's power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government," said Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants' Union organizing Saturday's protest.

Protests in dozens of cities

Police said around 70,000 people took part in the demonstration in Madrid. Organizers put the figure closer to 500,000 people.

Additional protests were held in around 50 other cities.

In the eastern city of Valencia, police used tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters.

Dozens of protesters had managed to get inside Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences — a major landmark in the city — before they were ejected by police.

What's next for the Spanish government?

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's proposed emergency measures included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants. However, bills were shot down by opposition parties on Friday.

This defeat infuriated those who had been protesting against the country's increasingly unaffordable housing market all week.

"We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project," another protester in Madrid, aged 31, told the AFP news agency.

Spanish media reported that Sanchez might call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass, adding that the government would be watching Saturday's protests closely before making a decion.

Sahcnez's office declined to comment on the reports.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Greece returns remains of Czar Samuel to Bulgaria
entries.summary: A warrior emperor who ruled the Bulgarian Empire in the Middle Ages, Czar Samuel is a symbol of Bulgarian national identity. But his remains have been in Greece for decades – and he is also claimed by North Macedonia.
entries.content:
October 3, 2026

A warrior emperor who ruled the Bulgarian Empire in the Middle Ages, Czar Samuel is a symbol of Bulgarian national identity. But his remains have been in Greece for decades – and he is also claimed by North Macedonia.

The remains of one of Bulgaria's most important medieval rulers were set to arrive in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on Saturday after decades of negotiations with neighboring Greece.

Czar Samuel ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, gradually extending his authority over a swathe of the Balkans as far south as Lake Ohrid, now in North Macedonia on the border with Albania.

But Samuel's rule was also characterized by conflict with the Byzantine Empire which ultimately defeated his army at the Battle of Kleidion in 1014.

Samuel is said to have died of shock when thousands of his defeated soldiers returned home having been blinded by order of Byzantine Emperor Basil II, known as Boulgaroktonos – the "Bulgar Slayer."

The Bulgarian lands fell under Byzantine rule four years later but Czar Samuel is still considered a symbol of Bulgarian national identity today, and his remains – discovered in a Greek border area 60 years ago – are set to be received with full state honors.

They are set to be flown to Sofia aboard a military aircraft accompanied by a fighter jet escort before a 21-gun salute and a procession to the Church of St. Sophia, where the public will be able to pay respects.

Free trains to the capital are being provided for the occasion, with some 750 police on duty during the handover ceremony.

Bulgaria: 'Czar Samuel unites us'

"These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve and must have the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestors," said Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev at a ceremony held at Museum of Byzantine Civilization in Thessaloniki, Greece, ahead of the handover.

Bulgaria officially opened talks on the return of the remains in 2007, and they became a major issue in relations with their southern neighbor.

"If, in the past, Czar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us," said Radev. "He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger."

Greece hopes for return of Parthenon Marbles

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, speaking alongside Radev, acknowledged that the remains of Czar Samuel have "incalculable cultural and spiritual but also emotional value" for Bulgaria, adding: "The global community is re-evaluating its long-standing stance on protecting cultural heritage."

In return, Greece is set to receive 48 sentimental objects pillaged by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during the First World War.

Some prominent Greek academics and religious leaders have criticized the exchange as inadequate on the Bulgarian side, but Mitsotakis said he hoped Saturday's ceremony would bolster Greece's international campaign to return the Parthenon Marbles, a collection of 2,500-year-old marble sculptures taken from the Acropolis in Athens and later displayed in the British Museum.

"This shift is embodied by today's initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation."

Czar Samuel: does North Macedonia also have a claim?

However, Bulgaria is not the only country to claim Czar Samuel, who is also celebrated with a huge statue in Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia.

"The bones return, the conflict remains! Samuel once again [contested] between Skopje and Sofia!" declared the Albanian-language newspaper Koha, while Skopje daily Sloboden Pechat called the handover another "battle over history."

In 2022, a bilateral commission recommended that Samuel be presented as the head of a state that "most contemporary historiographers consider to be the Bulgarian Empire" – territory which is now North Macedonia.

"Samuel occupies an important place in the historical narrative both in Bulgaria and in North Macedonia," Dimitar Bechev, a researcher at the Carnegie Europe think tank, told the AFP news agency.

Indeed, history has been playing a major role in the run-up to this month's Bulgarian presidential election, with incumbent President Iliana Iotova, backed by Prime Minister Radev, promoting a more neutral position between the European Union and NATO – both of which Bulgaria belongs to – and Russia.

"Radev is looking to attract the patriotic electorate," said analyst Bechev, adding that the return of the remains to Sofia "aims to underline the Bulgarian character of the Slavic population of Macedonia."

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Spain: Floods leave 102-year-old woman dead in southeast
entries.summary: Authorities in Spain rescued some 90 people after heavy rain sparked flooding in the town of Madrigueras. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez expressed his condolences to the family of a 102-year-old woman who died.
entries.content:
Spain

Spain floods: One dead, dozens rescued in southeast

October 3, 2026

Authorities in Spain rescued some 90 people after heavy rain sparked flooding in the town of Madrigueras. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez expressed his condolences to the family of a 102-year-old woman who died.

Floods in the Spanish southeastern town of Madrigueras have killed an 102-year-old woman, regional authorities said. 

Madrigueras, which has a population of around 4,000 residents, is located near the city of Albacete in the Spanish autonomous community of Castilla-La Mancha.

Authorities said 90 people had to be rescued due to flooding in the town.

Local Spanish media said the elderly woman was found dead in her home after the floodwaters had reached a depth of one meter (3.2 feet).

The floods in the region were caused by persistent torrential rainfall on Friday. Spanish authorities said around 140 liters of rainfall per square meter came down in Madrigueras.

Sanchez: Spanish government monitoring flood situation

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, in a post on X, said his government is monitoring the situation. He also expressed his regards to the family of the woman who died in the flooding in Madrigueras. 

Spanish meteorological authorities said heavy rainfall is expected to continue in eastern Spain through Sunday.

The torrential rain and flooding comes after the Mediterranean country witnessed its hottest summer on record this year.

Deadly wildfires were reported in Spain's north and south in recent months due to frequent hot, dry conditions.   

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: On German Unity Day, Steinmeier laments 'bitter setbacks'
entries.summary: Germany's president has used his final Unity Day speech to warn the hopes of the reunification era have suffered "bitter setbacks." DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

On German Unity Day, Steinmeier laments 'bitter setbacks'

Published October 3, 2026last updated October 3, 2026

Germany's president has used his final Unity Day speech to warn the hopes of the reunification era have suffered "bitter setbacks." DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Germany's leaders have gathered in the northern city of Bremen for official festivities marking Unity Day
  • German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier warned that Germany's democracy is being challenged again, pointing to the threat from right-wing extremism
  • In his final Unity Day speech as president, Steinmeier said some of the hopes surrounding reunification have not been fulfilled
  • The national holiday commemorates October 3, 1990, when the former East Germany joined the Federal Republic of Germany
  • Eastern Germany commissioner Elisabeth Kaiser says the country's next president should come from the east, and be a woman
  • She says eastern Germans remain underrepresented in positions of power more than three decades after reunification

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, October 3, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Thousands attend anti-war demonstrations in Berlin, Stuttgart

Thousands attend anti-war demonstrations in Berlin, Stuttgart

Thousands of people protested against war, military buildup and possible conscription in Berlin and Stuttgart on Saturday.

Among other things, the protesters called for a end to all economic sanctions and arms shipments, calling instead for increased social spending.

Protesters in Berlin marched from the Brandenburg Gate through the city center. Police estimated there were 5,800 attendees while organizers put the turnout at 20,000 people.

The organizers in Stuttgart estimated a turnout of around 15,000 people. However, dpa journalists who were present at the demonstration estimated the turnout to be in the low to mid thousands.

Skip next section After Bremen, Düsseldorf next up to host German Unity Day

After Bremen, Düsseldorf next up to host German Unity Day

Düsseldorf has been announced as the host city for next year's official commemoration of German Unity Day.

The annual event is hosted by whichever state holds the rotating presidency of the upper house of Germany's parliament, known as the Bundesrat. In 2027, it will be held by Germany's most populous state, North Rhine-Westphalia.

Düsseldorf is the second-largest city in North-Rhine Westphalia, after Cologne. The state is also home to the industrial cities of the Ruhr Valley including Dortmund, Essen, Duisburg and Bochum.

The mayor of Bremen, Andreas Bovenschulte, symbolically handed the baton to North Rhine-Westphalia's premier Hendrik Wüst, who will take up his post as president of the Bundesrat on January 1.

"Togetherness, connection, and unity are never a finished task," said Wüst.

"Continuing to work on this, maintaining one's interest, and keeping the conversation going — even with people whose outlook might be completely different from one's own," he added.

Skip next section East German economy still trails west 36 years after reunification

East German economy still trails west 36 years after reunification

More than three decades after German reunification, the economy in the eastern states still lags beind the western states.

The five eastern German states reached just under 79% of western Germany's economic level in 2025, according to an analysis by the German Economic Institute (IW) released on German Unity Day.

The figure is based on an index designed to track eastern Germany's economic convergence with the west. It incorporates economic output per capita, productivity, investment, research and development, employment, unemployment and self-employment.

Although the east has made substantial progress since 1991, when the index stood at 51% of the west's economic development, this convergence has stalled over the past five years, hovering between between 78% and 79%.

The researchers pointed to large shortcomings in research and development (R&D) in particular. They found that the number of research and development personnel in the east was equivalent to just over 46% of the same workforce in the west.

The researchers also noted that demographic change could affect economic convergence between the east and the west.

Without immigration, eastern Germany's population will shrink by more than a fifth by 2045. This would make it particularly dependent on skilled migration.

But the German Economic Institute noted that support for the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany party (AfD) in recent state elections has called into question the region's openness to migration.

Skip next section Oktoberfest crowds surge toward 7 million mark

Oktoberfest crowds surge toward 7 million mark

Munich's Oktoberfest is on course for one of its busiest years, with 5.2 million visitors recorded through Wednesday.

That was around 700,000 more than at the same point last year, according to anonymized mobile phone data analyzed for the dpa news agency.

If the strong attendance continues through the final weekend, visitor numbers could approach 7 million. The record stands at 7.2 million in 2023, although that year's Oktoberfest ran for two days longer.

Good weather is thought to have helped boost attendance this year.

International visitors now account for around 31% of the crowd, six percentage points more than two years ago. Americans are the largest group of foreign visitors, followed by Italians.

Around 58,000 Italians attended during the middle weekend alone, traditionally known in Munich as "Italian weekend."

Visitors are also getting older. The average age this year is 46, with people aged 50 to 59 making up the largest group at around 23%. The share of 18- to 29-year-olds has fallen by 5.1 percentage points compared with two years ago to 21.5%.

Visitors spend an average of just over five and a half hours at the festival.

Skip next section WATCH — Does Germany's Gen Z still feel the East-West divide?

WATCH — Does Germany's Gen Z still feel the East-West divide?

More than three decades after German reunification, many members of Gen Z say the divide between eastern and western Germany is fading, but not completely gone.

Young people interviewed in Bonn and Eberswalde point to ongoing economic differences, stereotypes and political contrasts, including voting patterns.

While some feel eastern Germans remain disadvantaged, others say their generation shares the same concerns about jobs, identity and the future.

For many, growing up long after the fall of the Berlin Wall means regional labels matter less than a shared German identity.

Watch the full report here:

Skip next section Berlin parties move closer to coalition talks

Berlin parties move closer to coalition talks

Berlin's Left Party, Greens and Social Democrats (SPD) have agreed on a "joint path forward" toward potentially forming a new state government.

The three parties issued a brief statement after their second round of preliminary talks, saying they would bring the current discussions "to a conclusion" next week. They gave no further details.

The socialist Left Party emerged as the strongest party in Berlin's September 20 state election and is seeking to form a government with the Greens and the center-left SPD.

The Greens and SPD have demanded agreement on issues including antisemitism, racism and organized crime before they are prepared to begin formal exploratory coalition talks. Concerns over alleged antisemitism within parts of the Berlin Left have been a particular point of contention.

The parties have not said when they will meet again or whether the preliminary discussions will lead to formal exploratory talks.

Such talks would still fall short of formal coalition negotiations and are intended to establish whether the parties have enough common ground to negotiate a government agreement.

Skip next section German asylum applications rise but remain sharply lower

German asylum applications rise but remain sharply lower

The number of people filing first-time asylum applications in Germany rose in September compared with the previous month, but remained well below levels seen in recent years.

The Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF) received 5,276 first-time applications, according to the Interior Ministry.

That was 40% fewer than in September 2025 and 70% fewer than in September 2024.

First-time applications had fallen below 4,000 in both July and August, after around 5,550 were recorded in May.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union, said the longer-term decline showed that measures taken by Germany and the European Union were working.

"The significant decline in asylum numbers shows that our measures at national and European level are having an effect," Dobrindt said.

The number of subsequent asylum applications has meanwhile risen in recent months, partly following a 2024 European Court of Justice ruling concerning Afghan women.

The court found that the discriminatory measures imposed on women by Afghanistan's Taliban rulers could in themselves constitute persecution and justify refugee status.

Skip next section Stranded cargo ship finally leaves Düsseldorf

Stranded cargo ship finally leaves Düsseldorf

A cargo ship carrying Mercedes vans has finally left Düsseldorf for Rotterdam, five days after becoming stranded amid unusually low water levels on the Rhine River.

The 135-meter (443-foot) vessel ran onto a sandbank at the end of a harbor basin on Monday. Attempts to free it using its anchor winch and by shifting its weight failed.

It was eventually pushed off the sandbank by another cargo ship the following day, but returned to the harbor basin and remained there while some of its cargo was unloaded.

The vessel was initially carrying 160 Mercedes Sprinter vans produced at the automaker's Düsseldorf plant. After it was freed from the sandbank, 50 of the vans were unloaded to reduce its weight. It was later cleared to depart after water levels rose slightly.

The cause of the grounding is disputed. Harbor authorities suggested the captain had misjudged the vessel's weight and draft, while logistics company Mosolf blamed insufficient dredging and said the harbor was too shallow.

Mosolf said the original cargo weighed just 390 metric tons (430 US tons), compared with the ship's maximum payload of 3,500 metric tons.

Water levels on the Rhine remain unusually low following dry weather. The Düsseldorf gauge rose from minus 9 centimeters (minus 3.5 inches) on Monday to minus 1 centimeter on Saturday morning.

Forecasters expect largely dry conditions in the coming days, meaning a significant improvement in water levels is unlikely.

Skip next section Visitors stranded on Berlin tower after lift breaks

Visitors stranded on Berlin tower after lift breaks

Around 20 people have been left stranded high up Berlin's landmark Funkturm after a lift broke down.

About 15 people were stuck in the tower's restaurant, while another four were trapped on the observation deck some 126 meters (413 feet) above the ground, according to the fire service.

Firefighters escorted the restaurant guests down the stairs, with one person with reduced mobility brought down using an evacuation chair.

The four people on the observation deck were unable to use the emergency staircase, which has several hundred steps. Firefighters considered several rescue options, including using a crane.

The lift's manufacturer eventually managed to restart it in emergency mode, allowing the remaining visitors to descend at a slower speed.

The fire service operation lasted around 90 minutes. It was unclear how long the visitors had already been stranded before making an emergency call at about 9:40 p.m. (1940 GMT/UTC).

Skip next section Steinmeier warns German democracy faces renewed threats

Steinmeier warns German democracy faces renewed threats

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has warned that Germany's democracy is once again being challenged.

The 70-year-old used his final German Unity Day speech as president to reflect on more than three decades of political change.

"I thought everyone had learned the lesson from history, and now I see supporters of right-wing extremism seeking to erase the memory of the victims of the Holocaust," Steinmeier said at the official ceremony in Bremen.

"I believed our democracy was secure and now have to experience it being challenged anew."

Steinmeier, whose second and final term as president ends in March, said his expectations after the changes that began in 1989 had been greater than what ultimately became reality.

Those expectations had included greater progress for liberal democracy and for "the undeniable reason of international cooperation," he said, acknowledging that there had been "bitter setbacks."

Looking ahead to his successor, Steinmeier warned that the presidency was "not an office to be taken lightly."

He said promoting social cohesion and preserving the country's unity would become more demanding in the coming years.

The official German Unity Day celebrations began earlier Saturday with an ecumenical service at Bremen's St. Peter's Cathedral attended by Steinmeier, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and other senior officials.

More than 550 events are being held in Bremen through Sunday to mark the 36th anniversary of German reunification. The celebrations rotate between Germany's 16 states and are hosted by the state currently holding the presidency of the Bundesrat, the upper house of parliament. Bremen currently holds the presidency.

Skip next section Germany marks 36 years since reunification in Bremen

Germany marks 36 years since reunification in Bremen

Germany is marking German Unity Day on Saturday with celebrations across the country, with the main national festivities taking place in Bremen.

The national holiday commemorates October 3, 1990, when the five states of the former East Germany joined the Federal Republic of Germany, formally reunifying the country after more than four decades of division.

Following a service at Bremen Cathedral, political leaders and other guests are gathering at the Die Glocke concert hall for the official ceremony.

More than 400,000 people are expected to attend the public festival in Bremen, which runs through Sunday, with hundreds of events including free concerts, discussions, guided tours and exhibitions.

The festivities are being held under the motto "Many Strengths — One Country." Bremen is hosting the central celebrations because it currently holds the rotating presidency of the Bundesrat, Germany's upper house of parliament.

More than three decades after reunification, significant differences between eastern and western Germany remain, including in income, wealth and representation in senior positions.

Skip next section East Germany commissioner wants eastern woman as president

East Germany commissioner wants eastern woman as president

The German government's commissioner for eastern Germany has called for the country's next president to come from the east, saying eastern Germans remain underrepresented in positions of power.

Elisabeth Kaiser, a politician with the center-left Social Democratic Party, told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung newspaper that none of Germany's current top political leaders comes from eastern Germany.

"That can quickly create the impression that eastern Germans play no role in leading our country and are only sitting at the children's table," Kaiser said.

"I think the time is right for an eastern German head of state again," she added. "Why shouldn't the next federal president be a smart woman from eastern Germany?"

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's second and final term ends in March 2027. Germany's Federal Convention is due to elect his successor on January 30.

Joachim Gauck, who was born in Rostock and served from 2012 to 2017, is the only president from eastern Germany since reunification.

Kaiser also said significant differences remained between eastern and western Germany in income, wealth and representation in leadership positions.

"These differences must be overcome in order to truly complete German unity," she said.

ormer Chancellor Angela Merkel, who grew up in East Germany, led the country for 16 years but was never president.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

It's easy to forget these days, but this city on the Rhine River was once the capital of West Germany. Even after reunification on October 3, 1990, the government and parliament stayed here until the big move to Berlin in 1999.

And here's something else that's sometimes easy to forget: Germany has a president.

The chancellor runs the government, while the president has a largely ceremonial role. That's one reason Frank-Walter Steinmeier may not be a familiar name outside Germany.

But the job comes with an important role as a national voice — especially on days like German Unity Day.

Steinmeier is due to deliver his final Unity Day speech as president today, where he is expected to raise concerns about democracy and cohesion.

Meanwhile, attention is already turning to who should succeed him when his term ends next year.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of what Germany is talking about today.

Published October 3, 2026last updated October 3, 2026

The Cockroach Janta Party has called for a protest in Delhi if Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar does not resign. After the Indian men's cricket team struck gold, all eyes are on their hockey counterparts.

What you need to know

  • Cockroach Janta Party set for round two with march to Delhi on October 10 demanding election chief's resignation
  • India beat Pakistan in the Asian Games gold medal match in Japan

Skip next section We are pausing our coverage

We are pausing our coverage

India offered a strong show on the last day of the Asian Games, but we aren't done with sports for the day. A FIFA international friendly match between India and Brazil is set to kick off in Kolkata later today.

As I sign off to watch that, we will now pause our coverage for the day. But we will be back tomorrow with more on the latest from India!

Skip next section Indian men join women's hockey team in securing 2028 Olympics berth

Indian men join women's hockey team in securing 2028 Olympics berth

India's men's hockey team beat Malaysia 5-1 in Saturday's final to retain the Asian Games title, marking the first time the team has won back-to-back golds at the Games.

This came a day after India's women's team delivered one of the standout results of the Games, edging defending champions China 1-0 in Friday's final to end a 44-year wait for gold.

Forward Lalremsiami Hmarzote's goal in the 10th minute, backed by goalkeeper Savita Punia saving a penalty stroke from China's Zhang Ying before halftime, helped secure the win.

The victory was India's first women's hockey gold at the Asian Games since 1982 and also secured the team a direct qualification spot for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

Skip next section Pakistan summons Indian envoy over border killing of 2 civilians

Pakistan summons Indian envoy over border killing of 2 civilians

Pakistan summoned India's charge d'affaires in Islamabad on Saturday to lodge a "strong protest" over the alleged killing of two Pakistani civilians by India's Border Security Force (BSF) near the border in the Kasur district of Pakistan's Punjab.

Pakistan's Foreign Office said two unarmed civilians were killed and a third injured when BSF personnel opened fire in the Bedian sector on Friday, calling it "unprovoked and lethal force."

While there was no immediate comment from New Delhi, Indian media reported a conflicting account, saying the men were suspected of trying to enter the country.

Pakistan rejected any characterization of the men as "infiltrators."

The incident comes against a tense backdrop of a historically fraught relationship between the neighbors. It occurred a day after Pakistan's military publicly disputed an earlier Indian claim regarding a separate incident in Indian-administered Kashmir.

Skip next section WATCH — India's bought brides: women traded as commodities?

WATCH — India's bought brides: women traded as commodities?

States in northern India continue to face an abysmal sex ratio at birth, leading to a shortage of women in places like Haryana.

This has led to thousands of women from poorer regions being brought to the state and sold as brides, giving rise to a lucrative human trafficking trade.

Watch to learn more:

Skip next section India beat Pakistan by 19 runs to retain Asian Games cricket gold

India beat Pakistan by 19 runs to retain Asian Games cricket gold

India successfully defended their Asian Games men's cricket gold medal, beating rivals Pakistan by 19 runs in Saturday's final in Nisshin, Japan.

After posting 211-6 backed by Abhishek Sharma's 61 off 20 balls and a late effort from Tilak Varma and Shivam Dube, India restricted Pakistan to 192-6 despite a big knock of 96 off 51 balls from Hasan Nawaz.

Nawaz fell four runs short of a century on the final ball of the innings, when he was caught by wicketkeeper Sanju Samson off Dube's bowling. It marked Pakistan's first-ever appearance in a men's Asian Games cricket final.

The event also marked one of the game's fiercest rivalries played out on an unlikely stage: a converted baseball field in suburban Nagoya, where Indians and Pakistanis living in Japan queued for hours to fill the 2,500-capacity venue.

"I think this is never going to happen again, India against Pakistan in Japan," Pakistan supporter Umer Dar, a 26-year-old Nagoya resident, told AFP.

"Even if it's in Japan, the craze of India versus Pakistan is always there," added Tokyo-based India fan Afroz Khan. "Anywhere they play in the world, it's always crazy."

While cricket remains a niche sport in Japan, there has been growing local interest, as shown by India's first-ever T20 international against Japan last week, which India won by just two runs in a rain-shortened match.

Skip next section Pranavi Urs scripts history, wins Asian Games golf gold

Pranavi Urs scripts history, wins Asian Games golf gold

Pranavi Urs has become the first Indian woman to win gold in the Asian Games individual golf after she sank a nerve-wracking three-foot par putt on the final green to clinch the title by one stroke, finishing at 15-under par.

Teammates Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar celebrated by soaking Urs with water as her win was confirmed.

China's Yin Ruoning and Singapore's Shannon Tan tied for silver and bronze a stroke back, with Yin claiming silver after a playoff.

This is India's first gold in the sport since Shiv Kapur's men's title in 2002. Urs, Ashok and Dagar also came together to win India its first-ever team silver in the event. China won team gold, with Taiwan's team, featuring five-time major champion Tseng Ya-ni, taking bronze.

Skip next section CJP calls for mass Delhi march on October 10

CJP calls for mass Delhi march on October 10

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has announced it will mobilize a nationwide march on New Delhi next weekend unless Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns.

The call follows a protest at Mumbai's Shivaji Park that drew thousands of demonstrators despite police denying permission for the gathering.

A similar protest at New Delhi's Jantar Mantar saw several opposition politicians and student leaders being detained on Friday, which is also observed as Gandhi Jayanti to honor the birth of Mahatma Gandhi, a global pioneer of nonviolence.

"If Gyanesh Kumar doesn't resign, cockroaches from across India will march to Delhi and protest at Jantar Mantar on October 10," CJP founder and convener Abhijeet Dipke said in the statement.

"And if the Delhi Police tries to stop us, wherever they stop us will become our Jantar Mantar. Ours will be a peaceful protest. We will walk on the path shown by Mahatma Gandhi."

Calling on people to join the march to preserve free and fair elections in the country, Dipke called it "a fight to save our democracy."

The announcement follows a tense October 2, when Delhi Police detained more than 700 demonstrators, including former Delhi Chief Minister Atishi, from Jantar Mantar and surrounding areas, local media reported.

Police had denied permission for the Delhi gathering and imposed Section 163 restrictions barring assemblies of more than five people.

The CJP-led gathering in Mumbai's Shivaji Park also saw a huge turnout, including film actors and musicians, but did not face a similar violent crackdown from authorities.

It is the latest flashpoint in a months-long movement that began as online satire in May and escalated into repeated street demonstrations, including a July 20 protest where Delhi Police used batons to disperse crowds. It led to the resignation of India's then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in late July.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the big news from India this weekend.

The Cockroach Janta Party is back for round two, calling for the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The movement's leaders have announced that they will march to New Delhi's Jantar Mantar on October 10, just weeks after CJP protests led to the resignation of India's education minister.

Meanwhile, things are heating up in Japan as cricket archrivals India and Pakistan face off in the gold medal match at the Asian Games. India has posted a total of 211, setting up an uphill task for its neighbors.

For these stories and more, follow our live blog.
